book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different

chapters.relation: The editor's introduction ('hello.') recounts his own path from an Apple IIe through a PC interlude back to the iPod and iPhone, and frames Jobs's arc: a bold, brash entrepreneur of modest means who revolutionized computers, music, phones, and movies, yet was petulant, insensitive, and cruel, a 'barefoot billionaire hippy capitalist' shaped by Sixties counterculture and Eastern spirituality who set out to 'make a ding in the universe.' It presents the book as neither demonization nor hagiography but thoughtful, mostly philosophical examinations of Jobs's life, work, and cultural impact from many points of view.

Mahon reads Jobs's 'reality distortion field'—the phrase Apple engineer Bud Tribble borrowed from the illusion-casting Talosians of Star Trek's 'The Cage' and 'The Menagerie'—through the ethics of deception. He argues that unlike the Talosians' non-consensual illusions (trapping Captain Pike to breed slaves), Jobs mostly changed people's beliefs about what was possible rather than deceiving them, often believed his own claims (even about his cancer), and sometimes freed people from false beliefs as the 1984 'Big Brother' Macintosh ad dramatized, so the field that produced the 'insanely great' Stevenotes, the impossible Macintosh schedule, and Dilbert's Dogbert parody needed little moral justification—and made Jobs's revolutionized industries possible.

Biondi argues the 'counter-cultural capitalist' is no paradox: Jobs succeeded not as a Gordon Gekko-style greedy capitalist but through the creative individualism of the cognitive counter-culture—the garage techno-geeks—who pursued their own vision rather than the bottom line. She traces the greedy-capitalist stereotype to Glaucon's Ring-of-Gyges challenge in Plato's Republic (people act justly only from fear of punishment), Hobbes's restless desire for power after power, and Marx and Engels's picture of alienated wage slavery under capitalism, with Rawls as the toleration-only-if-redistributed alternative. Jobs's hippie exterior (drugs, fruitarianism, Zen) masked an entrepreneur who, in Rand's 'creative mind' mold, put a ding in the universe through products like the iPad instead of philanthropy.

Noel measures Jobs against the four cardinal virtues from Plato's Republic and finds him wanting: imprudent (NeXT, the Lisa), unjust (taking the GUI from Xerox PARC, 'more fun to be a pirate'), intemperate (cruel outbursts like the 'dogshit for icing' cake), with only a brash, mind-changing courage. Drawing on Aristotle's golden mean from the Nicomachean Ethics, Nietzsche's master-slave morality and his Will to Power line about the man who 'determines values' for millennia, and Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, he argues entrepreneurs are a breed apart whose real virtues are independence of mind, vision, and audacity—and that Jobs, the anti-social creator who would not fit in, changed the world precisely because the cardinal virtues were 'prison walls' to him.

Munkittrick argues that because personhood cannot be defined (trait lists like 'long-term planning' are circular) and behavior cannot prove an inner mind—as Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment shows—people have always identified persons intuitively, and Pixar trained Millennials to do exactly that. He reads the Pixar canon in three stages: Toy Story's self-aware Buzz as nascent non-human personhood, the Human-as-Partner films (Ratatouille's Remy and Linguini, WALL-E and EVE, Monsters, Inc.'s Sully and Boo, Up's Carl and Dug) as mutual recognition of persons across species lines, and The Incredibles as showing that even enhanced 'super-humans' face otherization—so a generation primed by these films will accept AI, animals, and uplifted beings as bearers of rights.

Hicks starts from young Jobs the 'little terror' expelled from third grade and asks whether he failed the school system or the system failed him, answering that America's entrepreneurs are produced by culture outside school—garage workshops, Heathkits, dirt-bike ramps, and parents who back initiative—rather than rows, rote learning, and standardized tests. He catalogues the entrepreneurial character traits Jobs displayed (informed creative judgment, ambition and integrity like the carpenter's hidden plywood, initiative calling Bill Hewlett at home, courage, perseverance through the Lisa, NeXT, and Pixar losses, win-win trade, leadership) and proposes risk-exercise curricula, Montessori methods, and programs like NFTE so schooling can deliberately cultivate the virtues of a flourishing entrepreneurial life.

Salvino casts Jobs as a billionaire egoist-visionary in the lineage of Adam Smith's insight that an entrepreneur's self-interest, not good intentions, best satisfies people's wants, Emerson's self-reliance, and Rand's virtues of independence and integrity—comparing Jobs to Howard Roark while noting his intuition was 'un-Randianly' unreasoned. Through Schumpeterian creative destruction (the automobile killing the horse-and-carriage; Wozniak's Apple I that HP rejected) and Deming's quality-first management, he explains Jobs's 'faster horse' contempt for market research, then rebuts the three standard ethical complaints—Foxconn labor conditions, his harsh verbal lashings, and his refusal to join the Giving Pledge—arguing Jobs did more good making the iPad than philanthropy ever could.

Krause and Parker take on the charge that Jobs 'didn't invent anything'—Wozniak was the engineer, Xerox PARC had the GUI, MP3 players and smartphones already existed—by deploying Ayn Rand's objective theory of value, which rejects both intrinsic value in things and subjective value as whim. On Rand's distinction between 'philosophically objective' value (the best possible by the most rational mind, e.g. technically superior PCs) and 'socially objective' value (the sum of individual judgments in trade, her lipstick-versus-microscope example), Jobs's genius was converting the first into the second—making ease-of-use valuable to the early majority with the iMac, iPod, and iPhone—so inventing is neither necessary nor sufficient for entrepreneurship, and Jobs deserves the wealth and admiration his market success brought.

Thomas asks whether the Apple II, Macintosh, and iPod were great products regardless of sales or great because they sold, and answers that market success is real evidence of value: each sale is a buyer's revealed preference in a voluntary trade, a stronger test than critics or focus groups, which is why Jobs's flops (NeXT, the G4 Cube) were overdesigned, overpriced failures of utility rather than quality. Against Hume's quoted doctrine that reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions (hunger strikers and Jobs's own vegan fanaticism defeat any basic-desire theory), he follows Rand and Philippa Foot in grounding value in objective human needs and capacities, so products designed for those needs—like the iPhone the Apple team built for themselves—could be expected to succeed.

Framed by Dickens's Jacob Marley, Walker asks whether Jobs deserved his posthumous accolades despite giving far less to charity than Bill Gates, and tests him under three frameworks. Aristotle's virtue ethics acquits him (character is judged holistically, and charity sits near the golden mean of open-handedness rather than being a checklisted duty); Mill's utilitarianism acquits him (his innovations maximized happiness and he violated no Harm Principle—though abandoning daughter Lisa counts as a harm); and Singer's drowning-child argument condemns him as near-morally-bankrupt for selling luxury gadgets while children starve. Kant both convicts (charity is an imperfect duty under the categorical imperative) and saves Jobs: treating the affluent individual as an end in himself, never merely a means to the destitute, blocks Singer's demand for giving to marginal utility.

Klein and Fundora trace Jobs's Buddhism from Reed College meditation and the seven-month India pilgrimage (reading Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi yearly) to the Zen minimalism of Apple design, arguing his temper tantrums, harsh speech, and reality distortion field do not disqualify him from being 'on the path' since Buddhism is a practice, not a creed test. They expound the Four Noble Truths (dukkha in its three kinds, via Thich Nhat Hanh), the Eightfold Path's Middle Way, and anatta—the non-self they compare to Hume's bundle theory of the self against Descartes's thinking thing—and read Jobs's strip-away-the-essence aesthetics, the three-click intuitive iPod interface that keeps users in the moment, the non-dualist marriage of art and technology, and his Think Different self-reliance as deeply Buddhist authenticity.

White argues Apple's 'Think Different' commercial packages together two distinct character traits: genuine independence, in Rand's sense of judging from the facts of reality (thirteen-year-old Jobs confronting his pastor with the problem of evil via the Biafran children—'Does God know about this?'—rejecting dogma at Stanford, killing the iPod's screen, bending Corning to make gorilla glass on schedule), and pseudo-independence that asserts the primacy of consciousness over reality (refusing to bathe because his diet 'prevented' odor, treating cancer with fruit juice, NeXT's impossible eighteen-month promise). Using Binswanger's 'fallacy of false integration' (the surgeon-and-murderer 'cutter' example), he charges the ad with merging the traits into one folder, so Jobs should instead be praised without qualification for his independence and blamed without qualification for his pseudo-independence.

Meyer reads Jobs through 'individualistic perfectionism'—the Aristotelian tradition (via Rasmussen and Den Uyl, and Veatch) on which flourishing is objective to human nature yet agent-relative, an endless striving unique to each person's talents rather than Kant's by-the-book categorical imperative applied impersonally to all. Jobs embodied this: the 'bicycle of the mind' faith that reason and tools extend human efficiency, practical wisdom weighing goods like friendship, health, and art through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, experimental self-discovery (Zen, calligraphy, fruitarian diets), and the exile-to-NeXT-to-Pixar-to-iMac arc of constant re-evaluation—so the right question is not whether Jobs 'was' a moral perfectionist but whether each of us keeps striving in our own key.

Iuliano asks whether it even makes sense to blame Apple (not Tim Cook or the board) for the Foxconn suicides, child labor, pollution, or tax evasion, laying out the two conditions of moral agency—autonomy and the capacity to know right from wrong—via the blameless wasp. He then canvasses the corporate moral agency debate: Peter French's Corporate Internal Decision structures, which filter employees' personal reasons into corporate ones (the dividend example), and List and Pettit's functionalist group agency, whose judgment-aggregation paradox (three executives, an environmentally friendly but harmful factory) shows Apple's moral conclusions can diverge from every member's—against Quinton's 'sum of its parts' reduction—so holding the corporation itself responsible plugs the responsibility deficit left when no individual is blameworthy.

Pardi argues Jobs lived philosophically as an existentialist: the 'Steve Jobs Roll Your Own Calculator Construction Set' anecdote shows design by touch and intuition rather than master plans, every detail of a product mattered because it belongs to a life narrative of 'making a ding in the universe,' and he avoided both Kierkegaard's despair (the gap between actual and possible self) and Sartrean bad faith—quoted from Being and Nothingness—by never lying to himself about his products, calling faulty work 'shit' and redoing it. Against him stands Bill Gates the pragmatist, whose utilitarian Windows-for-every-desk business and 'rationality only goes so far' humility embody William James's pragmatic method, while Jobs's Zune taunt ('we made the iPod for ourselves') shows the existentialist refusing to compromise authenticity for market share.

Cohen retells the DOJ ebook case—Amazon's $9.99 Kindle pricing, Eddy Cue's agency-model deals with the five publishers, the most-favored-nation clause, Jobs's warning email to James Murdoch, and Judge Cote's conspiracy ruling—to ask whether Jobs and other businessmen live and work to serve consumers or themselves. He argues antitrust law encodes the altruist-utilitarian demand that producers sacrifice their own goals to consumer welfare, and defends the Randian alternative ('your life belongs to you') on which Jobs, Cue, and the publishers were entitled to pursue their own happiness through their work, so readers inspired by Jobs's 'find what you love' Stanford challenge should reject the ethics behind antitrust.

In an imagined Walter Cronkite-moderated afterlife debate, Jobs opens with 'most technology is shit,' holding up the iPod as art-through-simplicity—design as the soul of the thing, thought down to its essence—while Heidegger answers from 'The Question Concerning Technology': the iPod's four Aristotelian causes (material, form, purpose, maker) work together as co-responsible bringing-forth, a revealing whose essence is enframing, which conceals the human when technology is treated as mere standing-reserve and cheapest utility. The dialogue converges on Jobs's washer-and-dryer anecdote and the Mercedes line: technology that reveals rather than conceals our being—useful and beautiful—keeps it serving humanity instead of mastering it, and Heidegger's Nazi past is flagged for the reader to judge separately.

Knepp asks why Jobs's 'simplicity is the ultimate sophistication' produced the friendly, MoMA-collected Macintosh (the face-like design, the inviting handle, the signed internals) but collapsed into the $6,500 NeXT Cube, answering with Žižek's reading of Hegel in Less than Nothing: the original idea is already self-contradictory, the failure of NeXT (the over-engineered perfect cube, the $100,000 Rand logo trying too hard to be friendly) is its symptom, and the iMac is the second attempt that only the failed first choice makes possible. He grounds this in Kant's Critique of Pure Reason—the antinomies and the phenomenon/noumenon distinction that Hegel radicalized into a world driven by oppositions—finding the dialectic everywhere in Jobs: two sets of parents, orchards and Silicon Valley, 'Apple' as both high-tech and organic, and a childish lowercase signature made with grand cursive flair.

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Russian-born novelist-philosopher (1905-1982) of Objectivism, defending reason, rational egoism, and laissez-faire capitalism.
holes.why: Chapter 12's case that counter-cultural individualism drives capitalism rests on Rand's 'creative mind' and her moral defense of capitalism in 'What Is Capitalism?'

holes.name: Personhood (moral personhood)
holes.what: The idea that rights and moral standing attach to cognitive and moral capacities rather than to species membership.
holes.why: Chapter 14 argues Pixar trained Millennials to intuitively recognize personhood in non-humans (toys, robots, rats, monsters), a concept the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Creative Destruction
holes.what: Schumpeter's thesis that capitalist innovation incessantly destroys old industries and products from within as it creates new ones.
holes.why: Chapter 17 frames Jobs's Apple, like the automobile against the horse-and-carriage, as creative destruction in action—the driving force of capitalist progress.

holes.name: Objective Theory of Value
holes.what: Rand's view that value is neither intrinsic to things nor a subjective whim but an evaluation of the facts of reality by a rational mind in the context of a life.
holes.why: Chapter 18 answers the 'Jobs didn't invent anything' charge entirely through Rand's objective theory of value and its philosophically-versus-socially-objective distinction.

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Acts that are morally praiseworthy to perform but not blameworthy to omit—beyond the call of duty rather than required by it.
holes.why: Chapter 21 asks whether Jobs's sparse charity was a moral failing by testing whether charity is supererogatory, an imperfect Kantian duty, or obligatory under Singer.

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Russian-born novelist-philosopher (1905-1982) of Objectivism, defending reason, rational egoism, and laissez-faire capitalism.
holes.why: Chapter 23 evaluates Jobs's character through Rand's virtue of independence, her primacy-of-existence versus primacy-of-consciousness distinction, and Binswanger's Objectivist false-integration fallacy.

holes.name: Functionalism (philosophy of mind)
holes.what: The view that mental states are defined by the causal or computational role they play in a system rather than by their internal composition.
holes.why: Chapter 25 needs functionalism because List and Pettit's case that Apple literally thinks, forms intentions, and can be blamed rests on corporate decision structures instantiating functional minds.
